title: A Rainy Tuesday on the Amstel
excerpt: The forecast said stay home. The river said otherwise. Notes from a slow, soggy, entirely wonderful ride south.

children.text: The forecast on Tuesday morning was a single grey cloud with three blue lines under it, which in Amsterdam means nothing and everything. By half past eleven the workshop had gone quiet. Two punctures patched, one wobbly wheel trued, a gear cable replaced on a city bike that had clearly spent its youth leaning against canal railings. I looked at the drizzle on the window and decided lunch would happen somewhere else.

There is a ritual to rain gear, and everyone who rides here has their own version. Mine goes: overshoes first, then trousers, because doing it the other way round has never once worked. Then the jacket, zipped to the chin. Then a cap under the hood, so the brim keeps the water off my glasses. Anna from the front desk watched the whole performance and said I looked like a very determined bin bag. She was not wrong.
I rolled out onto the street and turned south, towards the river.

Past the Magere Brug and Carré the Amstel opens up, and the houseboats begin. Some are tidy floating cottages with geraniums in window boxes; others are rusting barges with bicycles chained to the roof and a cat watching the rain from a porthole. Smoke curled from a chimney on one. Someone had left a single wet deck chair facing the water, as if its owner had just popped inside and would be back any minute to finish the view.

The rain was the fine kind, not falling so much as hanging around. It gathered on my sleeves in tiny beads, and the river took on the flat pewter colour it saves for weekdays in September. The bike path was almost empty. A rowing eight slid past, the cox's voice carrying across the water in short, damp commands, and then it was just me and the hiss of my tyres on wet asphalt.

On a sunny Saturday this stretch of the Amstel is busy with families, road cyclists in matching kit and people who have forgotten which side of the path they are meant to be on. On a rainy Tuesday it belongs to whoever bothers to turn up. That turned out to be me, a man walking a very small dog in a very large raincoat, and a heron that refused to move for either of us.

Just past the ring road the Riekermolen appears on the bank, an old thatched windmill with its sails furled against the weather. Beside it stands Rembrandt in bronze, sketchbook in hand, looking out over the same stretch of river he drew nearly four hundred years ago. I stopped and stood next to him for a minute. Water ran off the brim of his hat and off mine. Neither of us said much.
Rain doesn't ruin a ride. It just edits out everyone who was only there for the weather.

Rain sharpens everything. The grass along the dike was so green it looked fake. The smell of wet earth came in waves. Every sound felt closer: sheep complaining in a field, the drip from the willows, the low throb of a barge engine somewhere behind me. When you ride in the sun you look at things. When you ride in the rain you notice them, which is not quite the same.

Ouderkerk aan de Amstel arrived the way villages do out here: a church spire first, then a bridge, then a row of cafés along the water. I leaned the bike against a railing, dripped my way into the nearest one and ordered a coffee and a slice of apple cake roughly the size of a paving stone. The woman behind the counter looked at the puddle forming around my shoes and said, kindly, that I must be from the city. I sat by the window and watched the river go by, grey and patient, for rather longer than a lunch break strictly allows.
The ride home was wetter than the ride out. It did not matter. I got back to the workshop with soaked gloves, a pink face and the unmistakable feeling of having got away with something.

I have ridden that stretch of the Amstel dozens of times in good weather, and I could not tell you much about any of those days. That Tuesday, I remember everything. I think bad-weather rides stick because they ask a little more of you. You have to decide to go. You have to put up with the drip down the back of your neck. And in return you get a version of the place most people never see: quieter, softer, entirely yours.
So next time the forecast says stay home, maybe don't. Just remember: overshoes first.
